title: Reducing the Gate-Induced Drain-Leakage Current of Carbon-Nanotube Transistors by Subliming Dispersants with Back-End-of-Line Compatible Temperature
authors: Takumi Inaba, Yuichi Kato, Yoko Iizumi, Yasuhiko Fujita, Kazufumi Kobashi, Takahiro Morimoto, Toshiya Okazaki
abstract: Carbon nanotube field-effect transistors (CNTFETs) are promising for monolithic 3D integration with silicon CMOS circuits in back-end-of-line (BEOL) processes. Further reduction in off-state leakage is essential for practical applications. In this study, we develop a low-temperature cleaning process for CNT-deposited wafers using a sublimable CNT dispersant. The process is carried out below 250 °C, making it BEOL-compatible, and does not deteriorate CNT morphology or lattice structure, as confirmed by atomic force microscopy and Raman spectroscopy. As a result, gate-induced drain leakage current originating from residual dispersants is reduced by approximately one order of magnitude. In addition, improvements in on-current, subthreshold slope, and threshold voltage variability are observed after the cleaning process. This study demonstrates a material-enabled approach to improve the transfer characteristics of CNTFETs and provides a practical route toward low-power CNT electronics.
summary: This work addresses the critical challenge of high leakage current in CNTFETs for advanced electronics by introducing a low-temperature, BEOL-compatible cleaning method. By sublimating residual dispersants, the researchers achieved an order-of-magnitude reduction in leakage current while simultaneously improving the transistor's overall performance characteristics.
main_problem: The primary goal is to reduce the gate-induced drain-leakage current ($I_{off}$) in Carbon-Nanotube Field-Effect Transistors (CNTFETs) to enable their use in low-power, monolithic 3D integration (M3D) back-end-of-line (BEOL) processes.
main_result: A low-temperature, BEOL-compatible cleaning process using a sublimable dispersant successfully reduced the leakage current by approximately one order of magnitude while improving other device metrics like on-current and subthreshold slope.
method: The researchers developed and implemented a vacuum annealing process below $250^\circ	ext{C}$ to sublimate residual dispersants from the CNT films, followed by comprehensive electrical and spectroscopic characterization.
model_or_system: The study focuses on CNTFETs fabricated on silicon wafers, utilizing semiconducting single-walled CNTs as the channel material. The performance is critically dependent on the removal of residual organic dispersants (like FC8) left over from the CNT deposition process.
key_observables: Gate-induced drain leakage current ($I_{off}$), on-current, subthreshold slope (SS), threshold voltage variability, and the presence/absence of dispersant-specific Raman or IR peaks.
important_parameters: Temperature limit ($<250^\circ	ext{C}$ for BEOL compatibility), leakage current reduction (one order of magnitude), and the specific dispersant used (Flavin derivative, FC8).
main_assumptions: The cleaning process is assumed to be non-detrimental to the intrinsic CNT morphology or lattice structure, which was verified by AFM and Raman spectroscopy.
figures_summary: Figures compare electrical characteristics ($I_d$ vs $V_g$) before and after cleaning, showing leakage suppression. Spectroscopy (Raman/AFM-IR) confirms the removal of dispersant signatures while preserving the CNT structure.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for low-leakage CNTFETs for M3D integration. It details the novel, low-temperature cleaning process using a sublimable dispersant. Results demonstrate significant electrical improvements, confirming the removal of residues and the resulting enhancement in device performance metrics.
why_interesting: While the core physics is semiconductor device engineering, the precise control over surface chemistry and interface states at low temperatures is relevant to understanding charge transport in nanoscale systems, which has parallels in open quantum systems where environmental coupling dictates coherence.
